evidence_description: User-controlled value passed as HTTP method to HTTPSConnection.request(user_input, '/'), enabling HTTP method tampering

IDOR in password update: the user_id is taken from the request body (data.get('user_id')) instead of from the authenticated token (current_user.id). Any authenticated user can change any other user's password by supplying a different user_id. No old password verification is required either.
User input matched against catastrophically backtracking compiled regex pattern r'((a)+)+' via pattern.sub(), enabling ReDoS

Arbitrary file read via path traversal. self.path from the HTTP request is concatenated to cwd at line 14 and opened at line 22 via open(path).read(). The regex filter on line 10-11 (r'/\.\.\/\.\./' with re.match) is trivially bypassable — it only matches a very specific literal pattern at the start of the path and fails for encodings, alternate traversal sequences, or simple variations like '/../etc/passwd'.

Bare except clause catches all exceptions (including padding errors from AES-CBC decryption) and returns HTTP 500 without logging. While this prevents stack trace exposure, the error response timing differences in AES-CBC decryption with unpad() can leak information about padding validity, potentially enabling a padding oracle attack (CWE-209).

Exception details returned to user in SSRF endpoint error handling: return {'message': str(e)}, 500. This leaks internal error messages, stack traces, and potentially internal network information (hostname resolution errors, connection refused on internal ports, etc.) to the attacker.

Missing function-level access control. The admin page is served to anyone who passes ?action=admin in the GET parameter with no authentication or authorization check. Any user can access the admin template by simply adding the query parameter.
User-controlled file path passed directly to bz2.open(user_input), enabling arbitrary file read via path traversal

Multiple hardcoded credentials in create_db() function. User accounts with plaintext passwords are hardcoded in source: admin/admin (line 140), test-user/test@123 (line 141), sagar/lall0l (line 142), alias/ohrealli (line 143), jacky/st40ngp@55 (line 144), sam/tomTOM123 (line 145), maxi/D@ni3lDizaark (line 146), lelol/Leeee@Looo@!$ (line 147). These credentials are exposed in source control.

NOT VULNERABLE. SessionHijacking.run() uses parameterized query: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE session = ?", [session]). The session value from the cookie is bound via placeholder, preventing SQL injection.

NOT VULNERABLE: The name from the URL path is validated against TRIGGER_MAP keys at line 81 ('if name not in TRIGGER_MAP: raise NotFound()') and then sanitized at line 84 to ensure it matches exactly. This prevents path traversal in template resolution.

Reflected XSS via the 'name' query parameter. The user-supplied name value is directly interpolated into HTML content via f-string: content = f"

Hello, {name}!

..." with no HTML escaping. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript (e.g., ?name=). The response_class=HTMLResponse ensures the browser renders the injected content.

Session fixation in SessionFixation.run(). The 'session' parameter from the request is directly set as the SESSIONID cookie: cookie['SESSIONID'] = session. An attacker can send a victim a link with a pre-set session ID, then hijack the session after the victim authenticates.

SQL injection via f-string interpolation of all user-supplied fields (name, username, password, address, email, contact) into an INSERT SQL query. All fields from the User model body are directly embedded in the query string without parameterization.

Insecure YAML deserialization via yaml.load() without a safe Loader on user-uploaded YAML file. PyYAML 3.12's yaml.load() defaults to the full Loader which can instantiate arbitrary Python objects, enabling remote code execution. An attacker can upload a YAML file containing !!python/object/apply:os.system directives.

Arbitrary Python code execution via eval(). User input from request.form['expression'] (line 116) is passed directly to eval() on line 120 with no sanitization: str(eval(expression)). An attacker can execute arbitrary Python code such as __import__('os').system('id').

Insecure SSL/TLS configuration in main(). Three dangerous SSL options are explicitly enabled: (1) SSLv3 re-enabled via ctx.options &= ~ssl.OP_NO_SSLv3 (vulnerable to POODLE), (2) TLS compression re-enabled via &= ~ssl.OP_NO_COMPRESSION (vulnerable to CRIME), (3) cipher server preference disabled via &= ~ssl.OP_CIPHER_SERVER_PREFERENCE (allows client to choose weak ciphers).

The sql() view contains SQL injection-looking strings ("SELECT id from Users where first_name = ''; DROP TABLE Users;--") but these are only used as display text for the exercise solution. No actual database query is executed — the strings are passed directly to the template for rendering. The view only compares user input against an expected answer string.
Use of weak SHA1 hash algorithm via hashlib.new('SHA1'). SHA1 is cryptographically broken and should not be used for security-sensitive operations.

NOT VULNERABLE. Uses parameterized query with named placeholders: 'VALUES (%(title)s, %(description)s)'. The parameters are passed as a separate dictionary to cur.execute(q, {'title': title, 'description': description}). The %(name)s syntax is a psycopg2 named parameter placeholder passed separately to execute(), unlike the vulnerable Student.create which applies Python string formatting (% operator) before calling execute().
cursor.executemany uses parameterized query with ? placeholders — not vulnerable despite dynamic data insertion

Path traversal in file upload. The original filename from the upload is used directly without sanitization: filename = file.filename, then filepath = os.path.join(UPLOAD_FOLDER, filename). A crafted filename like '../../evil.py' would write the file outside the intended upload directory, potentially overwriting application files.

Jinja2 template engine configured with autoescape=False. This disables automatic HTML escaping for all template variables, making every unescaped template expression a potential XSS sink. This is the root cause of all stored XSS vulnerabilities (dvpwa-002 through dvpwa-006). The secure default should be autoescape=True.

User input concatenated directly into HTML response without escaping: template += '

XSS: ' + user_input + '

' in Bottle handler
User-controlled file path passed directly to tarfile.TarFile.open(user_input), enabling arbitrary file access via path traversal
User input matched against catastrophically backtracking compiled regex pattern r'((a)+)+' via pattern.findall(), enabling ReDoS

Insecure deserialization via pickle in UnsafeDeserialization.run(). User-supplied base64-encoded data is decoded and passed directly to pickle.loads(): pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(object)). A crafted pickle payload with __reduce__ achieves arbitrary code execution. Requires risk level 3.

OS command injection in ImportPaste mutation. User-controlled host, port, path, and scheme parameters are used to construct a URL that is passed to os.popen via helpers.run_cmd(f'curl --insecure {url}'). In easy mode, strip_dangerous_characters is a no-op. In hard mode, only ';' and '&' are removed, leaving backticks, $(), pipes, and newlines exploitable.
Login endpoint at /login has no rate limiting or account lockout mechanism, allowing unlimited brute-force credential guessing attempts

NOT VULNERABLE in practice: While os.path.join(TEMPLATES_LOCATION, path) could enable path traversal if called with unsanitized input, all callers construct the path from code-controlled values (TRIGGER_MAP keys or 'home' literal with '.html' suffix). The WSGI app explicitly sanitizes the name against TRIGGER_MAP keys before calling get_template.
Cache-Control header set to 'public' without no-cache or no-store directives, allowing sensitive response content to be cached by intermediaries

NOT VULNERABLE. The parse_field() method validates the field parameter against an allowlist of valid_fields = ['ip_address', 'referrer', 'user_agent']. If the field is not in the list, it returns '1'. This prevents SQL injection through field name manipulation.

Passwords are stored in plaintext without hashing. On line 62, the registration handler stores the password directly from the form: User(username=request.form['username'], password=request.form['password']). The User model (line 26) stores passwords as plain strings with no hashing (e.g., bcrypt, scrypt). The `__init__` (line 30) assigns the raw value via `self.password = password`. If the database is compromised, all user passwords are immediately exposed.

NOT a real credential exposure. The reviewer_data tuple contains test/fixture data used for build_benefits_data() including 'auth_token' as a literal string value. This is test data internal to the application's data seeding, not a real authentication credential that grants access.

Cleartext password storage at signup. The signup handler index() calls User.objects.create(email=form['email'], password=form['password'], ...) at lines 24-25, persisting the user-supplied password from POST data verbatim. create() never calls the model's hash_password() method, so the password is stored in plaintext in the User.password column. Any read of the users table (e.g. via the over-exposing API in djangoat-047, the SQLi in djangoat-001, or DB compromise) exposes all passwords in cleartext. Distinct from djangoat-014, which covers the weak MD5 ALGORITHM inside hash_password() (user.py:131-134); here the write path applies NO hashing at all.

IDOR on note deletion. The /notes/<note_id>/delete endpoint does not verify that the authenticated user owns the note being deleted. While the template only renders the delete button for the note owner or admin, the backend has no ownership check — any authenticated user can delete any note by directly sending a POST request with any note_id.
Open redirect via redir parameter injected into meta refresh URL without validation

User input concatenated directly into HTML response without escaping: template += '

XSS: ' + user_input + '

' in Quart handler
NOT VULNERABLE: lxml.etree.parse(StringIO(xml)) parses a hardcoded XML string defined at module level (lines 5-17). No user input is involved in this XML parsing operation.

Django DEBUG mode is enabled (DEBUG = True). In production, this exposes detailed stack traces, settings, SQL queries, and local variables to any user who triggers an error, leaking sensitive information about the application internals.

Vulnerable to hash length extension attack. Uses SHA256(secret + payment_information) instead of HMAC for signing payment data. The naive secret-prefix construction allows attackers to append additional data and compute a valid signature without knowing the secret, enabling payment amount tampering.

Privilege escalation via mass assignment. The update_account function uses current_user.__dict__.update(filtered_values) to apply all form fields to the user object. The AccountForm includes an is_admin BooleanField, so any user can submit is_admin=y to escalate to admin privileges. The admin checkbox is only hidden client-side (template), not validated server-side.

SQL injection via Python string formatting. The 'name' parameter from user input is interpolated directly into the SQL query using Python's % operator: "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name}. The resulting string is then passed to cur.execute(q) without parameterization. An attacker can submit a name like "Robert'); DROP TABLE students CASCADE; --" to execute arbitrary SQL. Documented in the project README.

Missing authentication on message creation API: MessagesView.post() has no @login_required or @admin_required decorator, allowing any unauthenticated user to submit messages. Combined with stored XSS in the admin message view, this allows unauthenticated attackers to inject XSS payloads targeting admin users.

SQL injection via f-string interpolation of unsanitized username path parameter into raw SQL query: user_query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '{username}'" followed by db.session.execute(text(user_query)). Reachable from GET /users/v1/{username} without authentication.
Reflected XSS via unsanitized JSONP callback parameter allowing arbitrary JavaScript execution

SQL injection in AuthBypass.run() via the password parameter. The password is concatenated directly into the login query: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='" + username + "' AND password='" + password + "'"). While username is sanitized with re.sub(r"[^\w]", '', ...), the password parameter has no sanitization, enabling authentication bypass via SQLi payloads like ' OR '1'='1.

Race condition (TOCTOU) in transfer: the balance check on line 30 (current_user.balance < amount) and balance deduction on line 33 are not atomic. Concurrent requests can pass the balance check simultaneously, allowing double-spending beyond the actual balance.

Stored XSS injection point via unauthenticated API: message and from_user from JSON request body are stored in Message model without sanitization or authentication. Both fields are rendered with | safe in admin/message.html.
User-controlled URL path passed to HTTPSConnection.request('GET', user_input), enabling SSRF via arbitrary URL path

Remote code execution via eval() on user input. The 'class' GET parameter is passed directly to eval(): model = eval(classname). An attacker can execute arbitrary Python code by passing malicious input as the class parameter.

Path traversal via unsanitized username in file glob and path creation: Path('/tmp/').glob('vulpy.apikey.' + username + '.*'). The username comes from user input (via API key generation endpoint). A crafted username with path separators or glob characters could manipulate file operations. Additionally, the keyfile path is constructed without validation: '/tmp/vulpy.apikey.{}.{}'.format(username, key).
API login query uses parameterized query: cursor.execute(query, (username, username)) with query = 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ? OR email = ?'. User input is safely parameterized.

Excessive data exposure through unauthenticated debug endpoint. GET /users/v1/_debug returns all user details including plaintext passwords, email addresses, and admin status for every user via User.get_all_users_debug(). No authentication or authorization is required.
User-controlled file path passed directly to tarfile.open(user_input, mode='r:bz2'), enabling arbitrary file access via path traversal

JWT tokens are signed with the hardcoded weak secret 'just_another_secret' from Config.SECRET_KEY. An attacker who knows this secret can forge valid JWT tokens to impersonate any user on the API, bypassing authentication entirely.

Open redirect via user-controlled 'path' POST parameter. The path from request.POST['path'] is used directly in HttpResponseRedirect(path) without validation, allowing an attacker to redirect authenticated users to a malicious site.

NOT VULNERABLE: io.BytesIO(user_input.encode('utf-8')) on line 7 merely creates a bytes buffer from the user input. BytesIO itself does not deserialize or execute anything — the vulnerability is on the next line (pickle.load), not in the BytesIO call.

OS command injection in CommandInjection.run(). The 'domain' parameter is concatenated with the command name and passed to subprocess.check_output() with shell=True: subprocess.check_output(' '.join([command, domain]), shell=True, ...). Payloads like 'google.com;whoami' execute arbitrary commands. Requires risk level 3.

The /start_over HTTP endpoint resets the entire application database to its default state by calling helpers.initialize() (which runs python3 setup.py) without any authentication or authorization check. Any unauthenticated user can trigger complete data destruction by visiting this URL.

Weak password hashing using MD5. Passwords are hashed with hashlib.md5() which is cryptographically broken for password storage. MD5 is fast and susceptible to rainbow table and brute force attacks. Should use bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2.

When a SQL query returns multiple users, run_sql_query returns raw tuples containing all columns including password hashes at index 3: return {'users': _data}. Single-user responses (lines 155-160) correctly skip the password field, but the multi-user path at line 162 leaks MD5 password hashes. This is reachable via the GET /select endpoint.

SSRF in PathTraversal.run(). When the 'path' parameter contains '://', it is passed directly to urllib.request.urlopen(path), allowing the attacker to make requests to arbitrary URLs including internal services (e.g., http://169.254.169.254/ for cloud metadata).

Uses parameterized query for password update: c.execute("UPDATE users SET password = ?, salt = ? WHERE username = ?", (...)). The good version properly uses parameterized queries for the password change operation, unlike the bad version.

Sensitive data logged to stdout. The UsersHandler.post() method logs the full request body containing username and password credentials: print "POST ", self.request.uri, "\nBODY ", self.request.body. This exposes user credentials in application logs.
User-controlled value passed as HTTP method to HTTPSConnection.putrequest(user_input, '/'), enabling HTTP method tampering
User-controlled XPath expression passed directly to lxml root.findtext(user_input), enabling XPath injection to extract arbitrary XML data

SQL injection via string concatenation in SQLinjection.run(). The 'id' parameter from request is concatenated directly into SQL: cursor.execute("SELECT ... WHERE id=" + id). No parameterization or input validation.

Session IDs generated using random.sample() with Python's Mersenne Twister PRNG which is not cryptographically secure — PRNG state is predictable after observing enough outputs, enabling session ID prediction and session hijacking

GraphiQL access control bypass via client-controlled cookie. The IGQLProtectionMiddleware grants access to the GraphiQL interactive IDE based solely on the client-controlled cookie value: request.cookies.get('env') == 'graphiql:enable'. Since cookies are set by the client, any attacker can bypass this restriction by setting the 'env' cookie to 'graphiql:enable'.

Server-Side Template Injection via Jinja2. User-controlled 'name' query parameter is interpolated into an f-string on line 38 to build 'content', which is then passed to Template(content).render() on line 41. An attacker can inject Jinja2 template syntax (e.g., ?name={{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('id').read()}}) to achieve Remote Code Execution. The TODO in test_main.py lines 39-42 confirms this is an intentional vulnerability.

NoSQL injection via raw JSON request body passed directly as a MontyDB/MongoDB query. An attacker can send operator-based queries like {"username": {"$ne": ""}} to dump all users, or use $where/$regex operators for data exfiltration. The request.json() output is passed directly to get_nosql_users() with no validation or sanitization of query operators.

Detailed stack traces, debug information, and full server file paths are exposed in GraphQL error responses via the /graphiql endpoint. The format_custom_error function includes traceback.format_stack(), traceback.format_exc(), and the full filesystem path of the caller in the 'extensions.exception' field of every error response (except the initial GraphiQL access rejection).

NOT VULNERABLE to SQL injection. Customer.query.get(customer_id) uses SQLAlchemy ORM's primary key lookup which generates a parameterized query. While this endpoint has an IDOR vulnerability (documented separately), it is not susceptible to SQL injection.

JWT signature verification and expiration checking are explicitly disabled: decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False, 'verify_exp': False}). Any attacker can craft a JWT with an arbitrary identity claim (e.g., 'admin') without knowing the secret key, bypassing all authentication on the 'me' query.
NOT VULNERABLE: db_connection.executescript() uses a hardcoded SQL script string to create and populate the test table. No user input is interpolated into this SQL.

XSS protection explicitly disabled via response header. X-XSS-Protection is set to '0', disabling the browser's built-in XSS filter. While modern browsers have deprecated this header, disabling it removes a defense-in-depth layer in older browsers.
Safe parameterized query: conn.execute('SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id = ?', (post_id,)). This is the safe version of the SQLI app, using proper parameter binding to prevent SQL injection.

Weak Content-Security-Policy header. CSP is set to "default-src * 'unsafe-inline'" which allows loading resources from any origin and inline script execution, effectively providing no protection against XSS attacks. This is intentionally weak to enable the XSS attack vectors.
SQL injection via f-string interpolation of username query parameter into DELETE SQL query: f'DELETE FROM users WHERE username = "{username}";'. No sanitization or parameterization.

DEBUG = True in production settings. This exposes detailed stack traces, SQL queries, template context, and settings values to any user who triggers an error. The boom() view at /misconfiguration/boom deliberately raises an exception to demonstrate this information disclosure.

Uses parameterized query: c.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ?", (username,)). The good version's login function properly uses parameterized queries and Scrypt password hashing instead of string formatting.
Weak password hashing using MD5 during registration: password_hash = hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest(). Same weak MD5 hashing without salt as in the User model.
OS command injection via domain parameter concatenated into nslookup command with shell=True

Missing admin authorization on user update endpoint. Any authenticated user can update any user's data including setting is_admin flag via POST to /admin/<id>/update/. The User.objects.filter().update(**data) on line 66 directly applies all POST parameters, allowing privilege escalation.
X-XSS-Protection header explicitly set to '0' on all responses, disabling the browser's built-in XSS filter and making reflected XSS attacks more likely to succeed

CSRF protection is disabled. The csrf_middleware is commented out on line 27 (# csrf_middleware,) in the Application middlewares list. Although CSRF tokens are generated in templates, the middleware that validates them on POST requests is never active. This allows cross-site request forgery attacks against all state-changing endpoints. Documented as a vulnerability category in the project README.

NOT VULNERABLE: do_raw(user_input) accepts user input but returns an empty string. The actual XSS vulnerability is in the framework handler files that concatenate user_input into HTML, not in this trigger function.
XXE via xml parameter parsed by lxml with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False

Vulnerable to hash length extension attack. Uses SHA256(secret + payment_information) instead of HMAC for signing payment data. Same vulnerability as length_extension_attack.py — attackers can extend the signed message and forge valid signatures to modify payment amounts.

Missing server-side authorization on student creation. The students view handles POST requests to create students without checking if the user is authenticated. The template (students.jinja2) only shows the form to authenticated users, but the backend performs no auth check. Any unauthenticated user can POST directly to /students/ to create student records.
User input matched against catastrophically backtracking compiled regex pattern r'((a)+)+' via pattern.fullmatch(), enabling ReDoS

The login failure response returns a static HTML string: 'Invalid credentials. Try again'. Although this is raw HTML returned from the endpoint, it contains no user-controlled input — the message is a hardcoded string literal. No XSS is possible because no user data is reflected in this response.

Password exposed in API serialization: User.serialize property includes the plaintext password field (line 27: 'password': self.password). This is used in the /api/v1/users/ endpoint, exposing all user passwords to anyone with API access. Upstream sites of the same plaintext-storage flow: column declaration at line 11 (`password = db.Column(...)` with no hashing) and `__init__` at line 16 (`self.password = password`).

NOT VULNERABLE. Uses parameterized query with %s placeholder: cur.execute('...WHERE username = %s', (username,)). The %s is a psycopg2/aiopg parameter placeholder (not Python string formatting). The username value is passed as a separate tuple parameter, so the database driver handles proper escaping. This is the safe pattern for parameterized queries.

Safe parameterized ORM query. User.query.filter_by(username=request_data.get('username')).first() uses SQLAlchemy ORM's filter_by which automatically parameterizes the query, preventing SQL injection. The username from user input is safely bound as a parameter.
User input passed to yaml.load() with yaml.UnsafeLoader, which can execute arbitrary Python objects via YAML deserialization
User-controlled file path passed directly to bz2.BZ2File(user_input), enabling arbitrary file read via path traversal

Path traversal in ContentHandler. The 'file' query parameter is concatenated directly into a file path: io.open('read/' + file_name, 'rb'). An attacker can read arbitrary files by supplying directory traversal sequences (e.g., ?file=../../etc/passwd).

Password hash exposed in template context via auth_user_processor. The function calls get_auth_user() which returns the full User NamedTuple (including pwd_hash) and passes it directly into every template's context as 'auth_user'. This makes the MD5 password hash accessible to all templates via auth_user.pwd_hash. Additionally, NamedTuple's default __repr__ includes all fields, so any logging of the User object would expose the hash and PII. While no current template renders pwd_hash and no log statement captures User objects, the sensitive data unnecessarily crosses from the auth layer into the rendering layer, violating the principle of least privilege.

SQL injection via string concatenation in login query. User-supplied 'username' and 'password' parameters are concatenated directly into the SQL string: cur.execute("SELECT * FROM Users WHERE User ='" + uname + "' AND Password ='" + pwd + "'"). An attacker can bypass authentication or extract data with payloads like ' OR '1'='1' --.

Server-Side Template Injection in the error handler of /search endpoint. When the SQL query raises an exception (e.g., from a malformed SQL injection attempt), the exception message str(e) is interpolated into a template string via % formatting (line 280) and rendered with render_template_string (line 281). Dangerous builtins dir, help, locals are passed as context. An attacker can trigger this by causing a SQL error and injecting Jinja2 template syntax in the search parameter.

Django SECRET_KEY is hardcoded in source code: 'h++jszpm)i@p%ay_b=cp#()^od!qns14)h%@qm3)p=cuo+st^a'. This key is used for cryptographic signing of sessions, CSRF tokens, and password reset tokens. Exposure allows session forgery and other attacks.
CREATE TABLE statement is a static string literal with no user input — not vulnerable despite cursor.execute usage

The /api/me endpoint returns the full user profile including sensitive PII (SSN, DOB, full address) via current_user.get_profile(). The profile JSON is returned in its entirety without filtering sensitive fields.

The requests.get() call uses a hardcoded URL ('https://example.com'), not user-controlled input. There is no SSRF vulnerability because the target URL cannot be influenced by an attacker. Scanners may flag the use of requests.get() but the destination is a static constant.
Cross-Site Request Forgery on comment submission endpoint — state-changing operation via GET request with no CSRF token, allowing attackers to forge requests that insert comments on behalf of victims

XSS via unescaped output. The username variable (derived from decrypting a user-supplied cookie at line 26) is rendered into HTML without any escaping: bytes('Hello %s' % username, 'utf-8'). An attacker who controls the encrypted cookie value can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript.

Hardcoded Fernet encryption key: key = 'JHtM1wEt1I1J9N_Evjwqr3yYauXIqSxYzFnRhcf0ZG0='. This key is used to encrypt/decrypt session cookies. Knowing this key allows forging session tokens for any user.

Intentional exception raise Exception('boom') in a view with DEBUG=True. This causes Django to display a full debug error page including the complete stack trace, settings (with SECRET_KEY), environment variables, and installed middleware to any user.

File download via send_from_directory(UPLOAD_FOLDER, filename) is NOT vulnerable to path traversal. Flask's send_from_directory() safely resolves the path and raises a 404 if the resolved path is outside the specified directory, preventing directory traversal attacks.
User-controlled URL used to create Request(user_input) object then passed to urlopen(), enabling SSRF

SQL injection via f-string interpolation in login query: query = f"SELECT * FROM user WHERE username = '{username}'". The username parameter from user input is directly interpolated into the SQL string, allowing authentication bypass (e.g., ' OR '1'='1' --) and data exfiltration.

SQL injection via string concatenation: conn.execute('SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id = '+post_id). The post_id parameter is concatenated directly into the SQL query. The regex filter on line 67-68 (r'^\d+$' with re.M) is weak because the re.M flag makes ^ and $ match line boundaries, allowing multiline input like '1\nOR 1=1' to pass the filter.
NOT VULNERABLE: sqlite3.connect(':memory:') creates an in-memory database with a hardcoded connection string. No user input is involved in the database connection.

Hardcoded admin credentials at module level: USERNAME = 'admin' and PASSWORD = 'password123'. These credentials are embedded directly in source code, exposing them to anyone with access to the codebase.

SQL injection via string format in UPDATE statement: c.execute("UPDATE users SET password = '{}' WHERE username = '{}'".format(password, username)). The password parameter from user input is directly interpolated into the SQL query.

Path traversal in PathTraversal.run(). The 'path' parameter is passed to open() after os.path.abspath() which does NOT prevent traversal: file = open(os.path.abspath(path), 'rb'). A payload like '../../etc/passwd' reads arbitrary files. The only check is whether '://' is in the path (which routes to SSRF instead).
Hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY: app.config['SECRET_KEY'] = 'supersecret'. This key is used by Flask for session signing. A known secret allows session forgery.

Missing authentication on profile pictures endpoint. The /uploads/profile_pictures/<filename> route serves profile pictures to anyone without requiring login. An attacker can enumerate and access all user profile pictures by iterating over numeric IDs (1.png, 2.png, etc.).
User-controlled file path passed directly to open(user_input), enabling arbitrary file read via path traversal
Plaintext hardcoded passwords in USERS_XML constant including admin password '7en8aiDoh!'

Broken command allow-list due to Python string concatenation bug. The tuple ('echo', 'ps' 'whoami', 'tail') has a missing comma between 'ps' and 'whoami', causing Python implicit string concatenation to produce 'pswhoami' instead of separate 'ps' and 'whoami' entries. This means 'ps' and 'whoami' are not individually in the allow list, making the hard mode command filtering unreliable.

SQL injection via unsanitized 'filter' GraphQL argument directly interpolated into raw SQL using Python string formatting: result.filter(text("title = '%s' or content = '%s'" % (filter, filter))). An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL via the filter parameter of the pastes query.
Reflected XSS via v parameter injected into HTML response via re.sub without escaping

Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA). When vuln=1, get_by_title queries the book by title only (Book.query.filter_by(book_title=str(book_title)).first()) without verifying the authenticated user is the owner. Any authenticated user can read any book's secret_content by sending GET /books/v1/{book_title}.

Flask debug mode enabled in production: app.run(host='0.0.0.0', debug=True, port=5000). Debug mode exposes the Werkzeug debugger which can allow arbitrary code execution if the debugger PIN is guessed or leaked, and exposes detailed stack traces.

SSRF via urllib.request.urlopen(url). The url parameter comes from request.args.get('url'). The startswith('https://insecurewebapp.com') check on line 14 is trivially bypassable by using URLs like 'https://insecurewebapp.com.attacker.com/' or 'https://insecurewebapp.com@attacker.com/', allowing the server to fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.

Missing server-side authorization on course creation. The courses view handles POST requests to create courses without checking if the user is authenticated or is an admin. The template (courses.jinja2) only shows the form to admin users, but the backend performs no auth or admin check. Any unauthenticated user can POST directly to /courses/ to create course records.

BOPA (Broken Object Property Level Authorization) / Mass Assignment allowing privilege escalation. The update_profile endpoint accepts 'role' and 'permissions' fields from the POST form body (lines 187-196). Although these fields are commented out in the HTML form, an attacker can add role=admin&permissions=all to the POST request to escalate to admin privileges.

Global CSRF protection is disabled. The CsrfViewMiddleware is commented out in MIDDLEWARE_CLASSES: #'django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware'. This means no views have CSRF protection, making all POST forms vulnerable to cross-site request forgery attacks.

SSRF in the update_picture API endpoint. The server fetches a user-supplied URL via requests.get(picture_url) with no validation or restriction on the URL scheme, host, or port. An attacker can make the server send requests to internal services (e.g., http://169.254.169.254/ for cloud metadata, internal APIs, or localhost services).

SQL injection via f-string interpolation of user.address into DELETE SQL query without even surrounding quotes: f'DELETE FROM users WHERE address = {user.address};'. The lack of quotes makes exploitation even more trivial than the other SQL injections.

Arbitrary code execution via exec() on user-supplied base64-decoded POST data (Python 3 path): exec(base64.decodestring(bytes(first_name, 'ascii'))). Attacker can execute any Python code on the server.
Hardcoded encryption key: KEY = b'12345678910111212345678910111212'. This key is used for AES encryption of sensitive data (bank account numbers, SSNs). The key is trivially predictable.
User-controlled value passed as HTTP method to HTTPConnection.request(user_input, '/'), enabling HTTP method tampering

SQL injection via f-string interpolation of user-supplied search parameter into a raw SQL text() fragment: text(f"text like '%{search_param}%'"). The search_param comes directly from request.args.get('search') with no sanitization.
User-controlled XML passed to xml.sax.parseString(user_input, ContentHandler()), potentially enabling XXE attacks depending on parser configuration

Untrusted data from request.data is passed directly to pickle.loads() at line 33. An attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload to achieve arbitrary code execution on the server. The /unserialize endpoint accepts raw POST body and deserializes it without any validation.
The /lookup endpoint allows OS command injection but has no authentication check. Any unauthenticated user can access this endpoint and execute arbitrary shell commands via the address parameter.

No authentication required for password reset endpoint. The reset_password_handler and reset_password functions have no authentication decorator. Combined with the predictable token (djangoat-025) and pickle deserialization (djangoat-003), this enables unauthenticated account takeover and RCE.

API key generation uses Python's random module (not cryptographically secure): hashlib.sha256(str(random.getrandbits(2048)).encode()).hexdigest(). The random module uses a Mersenne Twister PRNG which is predictable. Should use secrets or os.urandom for security-sensitive token generation.

SQL injection via user-controlled user_id parameter: user_id = request.args.get('user_id', current_user.id) is directly interpolated into f-string SQL query on line 49. An attacker can provide a crafted user_id parameter to inject SQL. Also constitutes an IDOR since any user_id can be specified.

User passwords are stored in plaintext and exposed through the GraphQL API. The resolve_password method returns the actual plaintext password when info.context.json.get('identity') == 'admin'. Since the 'identity' field is set from an unverified JWT token (verify_signature=False in get_identity), any attacker can forge a JWT with identity='admin' and query all user passwords in cleartext.

Insecure direct object reference in EditPaste mutation. The paste ID is taken directly from user input and used to look up and modify the paste (Paste.query.filter_by(id=id).update(...)) without any ownership or authorization verification. Any user can modify any paste by specifying its ID.

Open redirect: request.args.get('next') is passed directly to redirect() without any validation. An attacker can craft a URL like /toggle_xss_protection/?next=https://evil.com to redirect users to a malicious site.

Plaintext password storage in User model. The password column is defined as db.Column(db.String(60)) with no hashing mechanism. The create_user classmethod stores the password directly without bcrypt/argon2/scrypt. If the database is compromised, all user passwords are immediately exposed in cleartext, enabling credential stuffing attacks.
User-controlled command passed directly to os.system(command) with no sanitization, enabling arbitrary OS command execution

The init_db function executes SQL statements with hardcoded string literals (CREATE TABLE and INSERT INTO with fixed values). No user input flows into these queries. Although the queries use string literals rather than parameterized queries, there is no injection vector because the values are compile-time constants, not user-controlled data.

Insecure deserialization via pickle. The Username.pickle() call on line 14 deserializes user-controlled cookie data using pickle (as documented in the commented-out code on line 15: pickle.loads(base64.b64decode(cookies.get('username').value))). Pickle deserialization of untrusted data allows arbitrary code execution via crafted __reduce__ methods.

Dashboard file listing query (when no search term) uses parameterized query: cursor.execute('SELECT filename FROM files WHERE user_id = ?', (user_id,)). This is the safe code path contrasting with the vulnerable search path on lines 137-138.
User input interpolated into SQL query via Python string format: EXECUTE_QUERY_FMT.format(user_input) then passed to cursor.execute(sql)

Predictable password reset token using MD5. Token is generated as user_id + '-' + MD5(email). Since user_id and email are often known or guessable, an attacker can forge valid password reset tokens and take over any account without needing access to the reset email.

OS command injection via the 'arg' argument in the systemDebug GraphQL query. User-supplied arg is concatenated into a command string: helpers.run_cmd('ps {}'.format(arg)), which executes via os.popen. No authentication or input validation is performed. An attacker can inject arbitrary commands (e.g., arg='aux; id').

Parsed XML content is rendered directly into the HTML response without escaping on line 169: '(parsed_xml) if parsed_xml else ...'. An attacker can craft XML that, when parsed and rendered, includes HTML/JavaScript that executes in the victim's browser.
User-controlled file path passed directly to io.open(user_input), enabling arbitrary file read via path traversal

The 'name' query parameter on line 19 is a string default parameter for the endpoint. Although it comes from user input (query string), it is only used in string interpolation for HTML output — it is NOT used as a URL target for requests.get(). The SSRF risk is in config.PUBLIC_IP_SERVICE_URL (an environment variable), not in the user-supplied 'name' parameter. A scanner might incorrectly flag user input flowing to requests.get(), but the name parameter does not reach that sink.
Default admin password hardcoded as 'admin' (line 14: password='admin'). The admin user is created with trivially guessable credentials. The login page even displays 'admin/admin' as the credentials.

The /sayhi endpoint allows SSTI/RCE but has no authentication check. Any unauthenticated user can access this endpoint and exploit the template injection vulnerability to achieve remote code execution.

OS command injection via os.popen(). The 'server' parameter from the POST request is concatenated directly into a shell command: os.popen('ping -c 3 ' + server). An attacker can inject arbitrary commands using shell metacharacters (e.g., '127.0.0.1; cat /etc/passwd').

No rate limiting on non-authentication form submission endpoints. The POST handlers for students, courses, and reviews in views.py have no throttling or abuse prevention. While less critical than the login endpoint (dvpwa-017), this enables automated data creation, resource exhaustion, and potential abuse of the application.
User-controlled code string passed directly to exec(code), enabling arbitrary Python code execution

No CSRF protection on any form in the application. Flask-WTF is not used and no CSRF tokens are generated or validated. The update_profile endpoint is the most critical: a CSRF attack could change a victim's role to admin, escalating privileges. All POST forms (login, signup, update_profile, upload, delete) are vulnerable.
User input matched against catastrophically backtracking compiled regex pattern r'((a)+)+' via pattern.subn(), enabling ReDoS

NOT VULNERABLE. The login query uses SQLAlchemy ORM's filter method with a Python equality operator: session.query(User).filter(User.email == form.email.data). SQLAlchemy ORM automatically parameterizes these queries, preventing SQL injection. The email value is never interpolated into raw SQL.

Log injection / log spoofing via user-controlled GraphQL operation names. The Audit.create_audit_entry method records the operation name from GraphQL requests into the audit log without validation. An attacker can assign an innocent operation name (e.g., 'getPastes') to a malicious mutation (e.g., deleteAllPastes), causing audit logs to misrepresent the true nature of the request and evade security monitoring.

Information disclosure via /is_logged_in endpoint. This unauthenticated endpoint exposes whether a user is currently logged in and their email address. Can be used for user enumeration and session state reconnaissance.

Critical command injection via custom HTTP method BDR in do_BDR(). The URL path (self.path[1:]) is passed directly to subprocess.check_output() with shell=True: subprocess.check_output(self.path[1:], shell=True, ...). Any command can be executed by sending a BDR HTTP request with the command as the URL path. Requires risk level 3.

Session fixation vulnerability. On successful login, the session ID is not rotated — the existing session simply has 'user_id' set (session['user_id'] = user.id) without creating a new session. An attacker who knows a victim's pre-authentication session ID (e.g. via the AIOHTTP_SESSION cookie) can hijack the authenticated session after the victim logs in. Documented in the project README.

IDOR leading to sensitive data exposure. The user_id URL parameter is used directly to fetch user data (User.objects.get(id=user_id)) without verifying it matches the authenticated user. Any authenticated user can view another user's work info including SSN and salary by changing the user_id in the URL.

Admin password 'admin123' is stored in plaintext in the database (user.password = 'admin123' on line 63). No hashing is applied before storage, unlike the /register/user endpoint which at least uses MD5. This allows anyone with database access to read the admin password directly.

NOT VULNERABLE. The Login mutation passes user-supplied username and password directly to SQLAlchemy's filter_by(): User.query.filter_by(username=username, password=password).first(). While this appears to pass unsanitized input to a database query, SQLAlchemy ORM's filter_by() uses parameterized queries internally, binding values as SQL parameters rather than interpolating them into the query string.

NOT VULNERABLE. XSRequestForgery.run() uses parameterized query for SELECT: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE session = ?", [session]). The session cookie value is properly bound via placeholder.

Hardcoded secondary HMAC secret: SECRET_KEY_HMAC_2 = 'am0r3C0mpl3xK3y'. While not directly used in the current code, it is a hardcoded secret in configuration that could be used in future JWT or cryptographic operations. Its presence in source code is a security concern.

The /evaluate endpoint allows arbitrary code execution but has no authentication check. Unlike the home route which checks session['logged_in'], the evaluate, lookup, xml, and sayhi endpoints are accessible to unauthenticated users, allowing anyone to exploit the code injection vulnerability without logging in.

JWT authentication bypass via weak/hardcoded signing key. The SECRET_KEY used for signing and verifying JWT tokens is hardcoded as the string 'random' (config.py line 13). An attacker who knows this trivially guessable key can forge valid JWT tokens for any user, including admin accounts, achieving complete authentication bypass.
SQL injection via comment parameter directly interpolated into INSERT statement with string formatting

Hardcoded Flask secret key: app.secret_key = 'F12Zr47j\3yX R~X@H!jmM]Lwf/,?KT'. This key is used for Flask session cookie signing. A known secret key allows attackers to forge session cookies and potentially escalate privileges.

Open redirect via unsanitized 'url' GET parameter passed directly to Django redirect(): return redirect(url). An attacker can craft a URL like ?url=http://evil.com to redirect users to a malicious site.

NOT VULNERABLE. Uses parameterized query with named placeholders: 'VALUES (%(course_id)s, %(review_text)s)'. The params dictionary {'course_id': course_id, 'review_text': review_text} is passed as a separate argument to cur.execute(q, params). The %(name)s syntax here is a psycopg2 named parameter placeholder, NOT Python string formatting — the key difference from the vulnerable Student.create which uses Python's % operator before passing to execute.

User input concatenated directly into HTML response without escaping: template += '

XSS: ' + user_input + '

' in aiohttp handler

Path traversal in StaticHandler.find(). The URL path is used directly in file open calls: open('./{}'.format(path), 'rb') and open('./{}'.format(path), 'r'). No path sanitization or directory restriction is applied. Requests like /static/../../etc/passwd (with an appropriate extension to bypass route matching) read arbitrary files from the filesystem.

Denylist bypass via batch queries. The processMiddleware only checks queries when info.context.json is a dict (line 95) but does not handle the list case (batch queries). An attacker can send a batch query (JSON array) containing denied queries like systemHealth, completely bypassing the denylist. Other middleware classes (DepthProtection, CostProtection) correctly handle both dict and list cases.
User input matched against catastrophically backtracking compiled regex pattern r'((a)+)+' via pattern.finditer(), enabling ReDoS

Hardcoded secret token. SUPER_SECRET_TOKEN = '5u93R53Cr3tT0k3n' is hardcoded in source code with a FIXME comment indicating it should be loaded from an environment variable. This token value is committed to version control and visible to anyone with repository access.

Password complexity check always returns True: def password_complexity(password): return True. This means any password, including empty or single-character passwords, passes the complexity check, enabling trivially brute-forceable passwords.
Use of weak MD5 hash algorithm via hashlib.md5(). MD5 is cryptographically broken and should not be used for security-sensitive operations.
NOT VULNERABLE: cursor.execute(SELECT_ALL) uses a constant string 'SELECT * FROM Character' defined at module level (line 3). No user input is interpolated into this query.

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via render_template_string() with user-controlled input. The request.path is interpolated into an f-string that is passed to render_template_string(), allowing an attacker to inject Jinja2 template syntax (e.g., {{7*7}}, {{config}}) via a crafted URL path that triggers a 404.

NOT VULNERABLE at lines 136-137: After initializing connection with user_input as host (which IS vulnerable, documented separately), the subsequent c.request(TRUSTED_METHOD, TRUSTED_URL) call uses hardcoded constants 'GET' and '/' — these specific parameters are not user-controlled.

User-supplied 'id' parameter from request.args is concatenated directly into a SQL query string: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = '" + user_id + "'". This allows classic SQL injection. The query is then passed to run_query() which simulates database execution.

Incomplete audit log sanitization allows sensitive data leakage. The clean_query function uses fragile regex patterns that only match token:"..." and password:"..." with specific double-quote formatting. Single quotes, alternate field names (passwd, secret, apiKey), whitespace between colon and quote, or other variations bypass sanitization entirely. Sensitive credentials can be stored in plaintext in the audit log table, accessible via the unauthenticated /audit endpoint.
User-controlled file path passed to execfile(user_input) (PY2), enabling arbitrary file execution and code execution via path traversal
The POST /reset endpoint deletes and reinitializes the entire database with no authentication or authorization. Any unauthenticated user can wipe all data by issuing a POST request to /reset.
User input matched against catastrophically backtracking compiled regex pattern r'((a)+)+' via pattern.search(), enabling ReDoS

The commented-out safe implementation on line 17 uses Jinja2 template variable interpolation: Jinja2.from_string('Welcome {{ user_name }}!').render(user_name=username). This passes user input as a template variable rather than concatenating it into the template string, so Jinja2 template expressions in the input would be treated as literal text, not evaluated. This is the correct and safe approach to template rendering. (Code is commented out and not active.)

Username enumeration via password reset. When the email exists, the response is 'An email was sent to reset your password!' (line 20). When it doesn't exist, the response is 'We do not have the email in our system' (line 24). This allows attackers to enumerate valid email addresses.
Use of Python's random.uniform() which uses Mersenne Twister PRNG, not suitable for cryptographic or security-sensitive purposes

Arbitrary code execution via exec() on user-supplied base64-decoded POST data (Python 2 fallback path): exec(base64.decodestring(first_name)). Same vulnerability as the Python 3 path but for Python 2 compatibility.

SQL injection via %-formatting in INSERT statement: c.execute("INSERT INTO users ... VALUES ('%s', '%s', ..." %(username, password, ...)). User-supplied username and password are interpolated via % string formatting into the SQL query.

Safe book retrieval with proper authorization (non-vulnerable path). When vuln=0, get_by_title first resolves the authenticated user from the JWT token, then queries Book.query.filter_by(user=user, book_title=str(book_title)).first(), ensuring only the book owner can access the book's secret content.

Clickjacking vulnerability in Clickjacking.run(). The /danger endpoint performs account deletion via GET request with no CSRF token and no X-Frame-Options header. The page can be embedded in an iframe on a malicious site, tricking users into clicking the delete button. The destructive action (DELETE FROM users) is triggered by a simple GET with ?delete=1.

No rate limiting on the login endpoint. The index view handles authentication via POST with no throttling, lockout, or delay mechanism. Combined with weak MD5 password hashing (dvpwa-008), this enables practical online brute-force and credential stuffing attacks.

SQL injection in /search endpoint. User-supplied 'search' parameter from JSON body is interpolated into a raw SQL query via Python % string formatting on line 261: "SELECT ... WHERE username = '%s'" % search_term. The query is then executed directly via db.engine.execute() on line 265. No parameterization or sanitization.

NOT VULNERABLE. The GET /find endpoint constructs the NoSQL query with a hardcoded key: get_nosql_users({'username': username}). The username string from the query parameter is used only as a value, not as an operator key. Unlike the POST /find endpoint, an attacker cannot inject MongoDB operators because the query structure is fixed server-side.

Parameter parsing concatenates multiple values for the same parameter name with commas via re.findall and join, enabling HTTP Parameter Pollution to bypass SQL injection sanitization on the login endpoint by splitting payloads across multiple password parameters

Server-side request forgery in ImportPaste mutation. User controls host, port, path, and scheme parameters which are assembled into a URL and fetched by the server via curl. An attacker can make the server issue requests to internal services (e.g., scheme='http', host='169.254.169.254', path='/latest/meta-data/').

View explicitly decorated with @csrf_exempt, additionally disabling any CSRF protection. Combined with the XSS vulnerability on the same page (|safe filter on qs parameter), this enables CSRF attacks via injected image tags to trigger gift card purchases.

User input concatenated directly into HTML response without escaping: template += '

XSS: ' + user_input + '

' in Django view

Cross-Site Request Forgery in XSRequestForgery.run(). The settings form at /settings uses GET method with no CSRF token. An attacker can craft a link or image tag that changes a user's email address: /settings?email=attacker@evil.com. The state-changing operation (email update) has no anti-CSRF protection.

Hardcoded Flask secret key: app.secret_key = 'super secret key'. This key is used to sign session cookies. An attacker who knows this key can forge session cookies, impersonate any user, and bypass authentication entirely.

Safe parameterized query: conn.execute('SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id = ?', (post_id,)). Uses ? placeholder with tuple parameter binding, which prevents SQL injection. This is the first (safe) version of get_post, before the second (vulnerable) get_db_connection redefinition.
SQL injection via id parameter directly concatenated into SELECT query without sanitization

OS command injection via os.system() with unsanitized file name. The uploaded file name (orig_file.name) is interpolated into a shell command: os.system('cp %s %s' % (full_file_name, bak_file_path)). An attacker can inject shell commands through a crafted filename.

Reflected XSS in SearchHandler. The 'q' query parameter is passed directly to self.render() as 'query' and 'link' variables. In search.html, these are rendered using {% raw query %} (line 70, HTML context) and {% raw link %} (line 71, JavaScript context), which bypasses Tornado's default auto-escaping. Additionally, X-XSS-Protection is explicitly set to '0' (line 88), disabling the browser's built-in XSS filter.

Server-Side Template Injection in 404 error handler. request.url is interpolated into a template string via Python % formatting (line 112), then rendered with render_template_string (line 114). Additionally, dangerous builtins dir, help, and locals are passed as template context, facilitating exploitation to achieve RCE.

Insecure CORS configuration: the server reflects any Origin header back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. This allows any malicious website to make authenticated cross-origin requests to the API, enabling CSRF-like attacks and data theft.

Mass assignment vulnerability allowing privilege escalation. When vuln=1, the register_user function checks if 'admin' is present in the user-supplied JSON body and uses it to set the admin flag on the new user. An attacker can register as admin by including '"admin": true' in the POST /users/v1/register request body.

Flask SECRET_KEY and JWT_SECRET_KEY are both hardcoded as the string 'dvga'. This allows attackers to forge Flask session cookies and JWT access/refresh tokens, enabling authentication bypass and session hijacking.
Path traversal via path parameter passed to open() with os.path.abspath but no path restriction
Remote code execution via include parameter: fetches arbitrary local/remote file and passes it to exec()

IDOR on message access. The message is fetched by message_id (Message.objects.get(pk=message_id)) without verifying the authenticated user is the message's sender or receiver. Any authenticated user can read or delete any user's messages by changing the message_id in the URL.
Passwords are hashed using MD5 (hashlib.md5) with no salt. MD5 is cryptographically broken and trivially reversible via rainbow tables. The function is used for all password storage and verification.
User input matched against catastrophically backtracking regex pattern r'((a)+)+' via re.split(), enabling ReDoS

Unrestricted file upload in UploadHandler. The handler accepts any file type without validation of content type, extension, or file content. The original file extension is preserved (line 62: os.path.splitext(original_fname)[1]) and the file is written to /tmp/. While the filename is randomized, the lack of extension/type validation allows uploading of executable scripts, web shells, or other malicious files.

subprocess.run uses a list argument (not shell=True): subprocess.run([program, username, password], stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL). While program and username come from sys.argv, the use of list arguments with no shell=True prevents command injection. This is a client-side tool, not a web endpoint.

Safe parameterized INSERT: db.cursor().execute('INSERT INTO comments (comment) VALUES (?)', (comment,)). The user-supplied comment is safely bound via ? placeholder parameter binding, preventing SQL injection.
NOT VULNERABLE: do_parameter_pollution(user_input) accepts user input but returns an empty string with no dangerous operations. The function is a stub with no actual vulnerability trigger.

Deep recursion denial of service via circular type references in the GraphQL schema. PasteObject defines an 'owner' field resolving to OwnerObject, and OwnerObject defines a 'pastes' field resolving back to PasteObject. An attacker can craft deeply nested queries like { pastes { owner { pastes { owner { ... } } } } } that cause exponential response growth and server crash. No query depth limiting is enforced at the resolver level in easy mode.

Redis config schema and connection code have no password support. The CONFIG_SCHEMA does not include a password field and aioredis.create_pool() in sqli/services/redis.py does not pass one. This architecturally prevents Redis authentication even if desired, leaving session data accessible to anyone with network access to the Redis instance.
User-controlled URL path passed to HTTPConnection.putrequest('GET', user_input), enabling SSRF via arbitrary URL path

Unauthenticated access to all user records via the resolve_users GraphQL resolver. When no id parameter is provided, all User objects are returned including sensitive fields (passwords via resolve_password). No authentication or authorization check is performed. Any anonymous user can enumerate all users and their data.
User input passed to yaml.load_all() with yaml.UnsafeLoader, which can execute arbitrary Python objects via YAML deserialization
XPath injection via name parameter directly interpolated into XPath query string

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) in /fetch/customer. Any authenticated user can fetch any customer's record (including credit card numbers) by supplying an arbitrary customer ID. There is no authorization check to verify the requesting user is allowed to access the specified customer record.
SQL injection via string concatenation: cursor.execute("SELECT ... WHERE username = '" + username + '"'). User-supplied username is concatenated directly into the SQL query string.

Path traversal via unsanitized 'p' GET parameter joined directly into file path: open(os.path.join(base_path, filename), 'rb').read(). An attacker can use '../../' sequences to read arbitrary files (e.g., ?p=../../settings.py to read Django settings including SECRET_KEY).

JWT signature verification is completely disabled. jwt.decode(token, verify=False) accepts any token regardless of signature validity. This function is used to protect the /get/<cust_id> endpoint (line 227), meaning an attacker can forge arbitrary JWT tokens to bypass authentication and access any customer record.

PARTIALLY MITIGATED but still vulnerable (see djangoat-030). The data_path uses os.path.join(settings.MEDIA_ROOT, 'data') which is a fixed base path, but the uploaded_file.name on line 33 is not sanitized. Note: os.path.join with an absolute second argument would replace the first, but Django's UploadedFile.name is typically relative. The real risk is in the filename containing traversal sequences. Documenting as FP for the data_path construction itself.
Weak hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY in SSL variant: app.config['SECRET_KEY'] = 'aaaaaaa'.

Passwords stored in plaintext in the database. User passwords from users.xml are inserted directly into SQLite without hashing: INSERT INTO users(..., password, ...) VALUES(NULL, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?). The password column in the users table (line 33) stores raw plaintext passwords, making all credentials recoverable if the database is compromised.

NOT VULNERABLE. The selected_id is cast to int() before being passed to User.objects.get(user_id=int(selected_id)). The Django ORM parameterizes the query. The int() cast prevents any SQL injection via the URL parameter.

User input concatenated directly into HTML response without escaping: template += '

XSS: ' + user_input + '

' in Pyramid handler

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) on the /accounts/<user_id>/notes endpoint. Any authenticated user can view any other user's notes (including private ones) by changing the user_id parameter in the URL. No authorization check verifies that the requesting user owns the requested notes.
The /xml endpoint allows XXE attacks but has no authentication check. Any unauthenticated user can access this endpoint and exploit the XXE vulnerability to read local files or perform SSRF.

Reflected XSS in search endpoint. The query parameter 'q' from request.args is directly interpolated into an HTML response via f-string: f"

Search Results for {query}

". No output encoding or escaping is applied. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript via the q parameter.

Hardcoded default admin credentials: username='admin', password='admin123'. These credentials are seeded into the database on first request and provide full application access. The password is stored in plaintext (no hashing).

Insecure direct object reference in DeletePaste mutation. The paste ID is taken directly from user input and used to delete the paste (Paste.query.filter_by(id=id).delete()) without any ownership or authorization verification. Any user can delete any paste by specifying its ID.
NOT VULNERABLE. User.objects.filter(email=request.POST.get('email', '')) uses Django's ORM with keyword argument filtering, which parameterizes the query. User input is not interpolated into raw SQL.

Remote code execution via insecure deserialization. User-controlled POST parameter 'user' is base64-decoded and passed to pickle.loads(): user = pickle.loads(base64.b64decode(encoded_user)). An attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload to execute arbitrary code on the server.

Authentication cookie set without Secure or HttpOnly flags in the signup auto-login flow. After creating and authenticating a new user, the index view sets the session credential via response.set_cookie('auth_token', auth.auth_token) with no secure=True or httponly=True parameters. This makes the auth_token readable by JavaScript (enabling theft via the application's XSS sinks) and transmittable over unencrypted HTTP. This is a distinct sink from djangoat-029, which covers the same weakness in the login flow (app/views/sessions/views.py); the scorer matches on file+CWE+line so the two locations do not overlap.

Hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY: 'Keep it secret, keep it safe'. This secret is used for signing session cookies. An attacker who knows this value can forge arbitrary session cookies, impersonate any user, and escalate privileges.

Broken API authentication via weak regex-based token validation. The comment on line 41 explicitly states 'This is purposely vulnerable'. The regex '(.*?)-(.*)' is overly permissive - group(1) captures everything before the first dash. Combined with the hardcoded ACCESS_TOKEN_SALT, an attacker who knows the salt can forge tokens for any user.
Uses parameterized query with ? placeholder: c.execute("SELECT * FROM posts WHERE username = ? ORDER BY date DESC", (username,)). The username parameter is properly bound, preventing SQL injection.
NOT VULNERABLE: tree.xpath('/planet[name[text()="Kepler"]]') uses a hardcoded XPath expression at module level. No user input is involved in this query.

Session cookie is merely base64-encoded JSON with no signing or encryption: base64.b64encode(json.dumps({'username': username}).encode()). An attacker can trivially forge any session by base64-encoding a JSON object with any username, achieving account takeover / authentication bypass.

DEBUG mode enabled in production code: app.config['DEBUG'] = True exposes the Werkzeug interactive debugger, which allows arbitrary code execution if the debugger PIN is known or guessable, and leaks stack traces, source code, and local variables to any user who triggers an error.

NOT VULNERABLE. XSSStored.run() uses parameterized query for INSERT: cursor.execute('INSERT INTO comments VALUES(NULL, ?, ?)', [comment, time.ctime()]). The ? placeholders properly bind the user-supplied comment value, preventing SQL injection. The stored XSS vulnerability exists in the output rendering (line 97), not in the database insertion.

Safe ORM query: Transaction.query.get(transaction_id) uses SQLAlchemy's ORM primary key lookup which is parameterized. The transaction_id comes from a URL parameter typed as int, and the ORM handles parameterization. Not vulnerable to SQL injection.
NOT VULNERABLE. Clickjacking.run() uses parameterized query for SELECT: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE session = ?", [session]). The session cookie value is properly bound.

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via urlopen(url) where url is user-supplied from the profile image URL form. An attacker can provide internal URLs (e.g., file:///etc/passwd, http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/) to access internal network resources, cloud metadata endpoints, or read local files.

Username ('admin') and password ('password123') are hardcoded as module-level constants USERNAME and PASSWORD, then used directly in the /login authentication check. Any attacker with source code access obtains valid credentials.

Plaintext password storage. User credentials are inserted into the database without any hashing: INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES ('user1', 'password1'). The password column stores raw plaintext, allowing full credential compromise if the database is accessed.

User and password enumeration via differential error messages. When vuln=1, login_user returns 'Password is not correct for the given username.' for valid usernames with wrong passwords (line 103) and 'Username does not exist' for invalid usernames (line 106). This allows attackers to enumerate valid usernames. Additionally, the except jsonschema.exceptions.ValidationError as exc: handler at line 112 returns exc.message directly in the 400 response body, leaking jsonschema-internal validator/path detail to the client.

NOT VULNERABLE: The _hash helper function simply calls hasher.update(b) and hasher.hexdigest(). The weakness is in the choice of hash algorithm (MD5/SHA1) made by the caller, not in the update/hexdigest operations themselves.

Unsafe function dispatch via globals().get(forward) using user-supplied 'fwd' GET parameter. An attacker can call any function in the module's global scope by name (e.g., ?fwd=admin to access the admin view, or ?fwd=boom to trigger errors). This is an unvalidated forward vulnerability.

XXE vulnerability via docx file upload on /xxe_uploader endpoint. User-uploaded .docx files are parsed with python-docx's Document() (line 303). DOCX files are ZIP archives containing XML. With python-docx 0.8.5 and lxml 4.2.1, maliciously crafted OOXML documents with external entity references can be processed. The endpoint is explicitly named 'xxe' indicating intentional vulnerability. An attacker can craft a docx with embedded XXE payloads to read local files or perform SSRF.

Mass assignment vulnerability. All POST parameters are passed directly to User.objects.filter().update(**data) without filtering allowed fields. An attacker can set arbitrary model fields including is_admin, auth_token, user_id, etc.

Missing CSRF protection. The Application settings do not include 'xsrf_cookies': True, and no CSRF tokens are used in any forms (login, upload, server ping). This allows cross-site request forgery attacks against all POST endpoints.

Hardcoded Flask secret key: app.config['SECRET_KEY'] = 'qwerty12345'. This weak, predictable secret key allows attackers to forge session cookies and CSRF tokens, potentially leading to session hijacking.
Remote code execution via eval() on user input. The 'class' GET parameter is passed directly to eval(): model = eval(classname). Same vulnerability as api_index but in a different endpoint (api_id).

Hardcoded user credentials in seed data including admin password 'admin1234' (line 16) and other user passwords ('yankeessuck', 'alohaowasp', 'motocross1445', 'citrusblend'). These are default credentials that would be present in any deployment using the seed command.

Insecure session management via plain cookie. The session cookie is set with response.set_cookie('session', username) with no HttpOnly flag, no Secure flag, no SameSite attribute, and the value is the raw username (not a signed/encrypted session token). This allows cookie theft via XSS, session spoofing by setting arbitrary cookie values, and transmission over unencrypted connections.
Not vulnerable to SQL injection: User.query.filter_by(id=user_id) uses SQLAlchemy ORM with parameterized queries. The user_id from Flask-Login's session is safely bound.

Weak identifier generation. The generate_uuid function truncates UUID4 values to only 6 hex characters (str(uuid.uuid4())[0:6]), providing ~16.7 million possible values instead of the full 2^122 UUID4 space. This makes resource identifiers brute-forceable, enabling IDOR attacks against resources that rely on these short IDs for access control.

MFA disable endpoint uses GET method with no CSRF protection and no re-authentication: @mod_mfa.route('/disable', methods=['GET']). Any authenticated user can have their MFA disabled via a simple GET request, which can be triggered by an attacker via CSRF (e.g., an img tag or link).

Database DSN constructed via string formatting with plaintext password. The _init_pg function builds a DSN string by interpolating config values including the password: 'password={password}'.format(**conf). However, the DSN is a local variable used only during startup, is not logged by any code path, and is not exposed via error pages (startup errors occur before the HTTP server runs). Standard Python tracebacks show source lines, not interpolated variable values. The password already exists in cleartext in the config YAML and app['config']['db'] dict, making the DSN no more risky. Using keyword arguments to aiopg.create_pool() would be marginally better defensive practice.

No server-side session invalidation on logout: the logout endpoint returns a success message but the JWT token remains valid. There is no token blacklist or revocation mechanism, so a stolen token continues to work after the user logs out.

Arbitrary file read via path traversal. The 'name' GET parameter is concatenated directly to BASE_DIR without sanitization: path = BASE_DIR + r'/' + request.GET.get('name', ''). An attacker can use '../' sequences to read any file on the filesystem.
Signup INSERT query uses parameterized query with ? placeholders: cursor.execute(query, (username, email, country, hashed_password)). User-supplied values are safely parameterized.
User-controlled URL path passed to HTTPSConnection.putrequest('GET', user_input), enabling SSRF via arbitrary URL path

Passwords are hashed using unsalted MD5: md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest(). MD5 is cryptographically broken and unsuitable for password storage. The lack of salt means identical passwords produce identical hashes, enabling rainbow table attacks and statistical analysis. Passwords should use bcrypt, argon2, or PBKDF2. Documented in the project README.

NOT VULNERABLE at this line: PATTERN = r'((a)+)+' is just a string constant definition. The vulnerability only materializes when this pattern is used with user-controlled input in the re.* functions below. The pattern definition itself is not a vulnerability.

Unauthorized password change (IDOR). When vuln=1, the update_password function uses the username from the URL path parameter to look up the user whose password to change, instead of using the authenticated user from the JWT token (resp['sub']). Any authenticated user can change any other user's password by sending PUT /users/v1/{victim_username}/password.
Hardcoded JWT signing secret: jwt.encode(..., 'secret', algorithm='HS256'). The trivially guessable secret 'secret' allows any attacker to forge valid JWT tokens and impersonate any user.

NOT VULNERABLE. Passwords are properly hashed using bcrypt with a random salt: hashpw(form.password.data.encode('utf-8'), gensalt()). bcrypt is a strong, adaptive hashing algorithm suitable for password storage. The same secure pattern is used in account updates (routes/account.py:88).

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR). User profiles are accessed and modified by sequential numeric userid in URL (/direct-object-references/users/1, /users/2) with no authentication or authorization checks. Any user can view and modify any other user's profile data by changing the userid parameter.

SQL injection via string formatting in raw query. Both ip and col parameters are interpolated directly into SQL: 'SELECT %s FROM %s WHERE ip_address=\'%s\' ORDER BY id DESC' % (col, table_name, ip). The ip parameter comes from request.GET['ip'] in admin_analytics view, and the col parameter is constructed from GET parameter keys.

Safe parameterized INSERT: conn.execute('INSERT INTO posts (title, content) VALUES (?, ?)', (title, content)). Uses ? placeholders with tuple parameter binding. User-supplied title and content from request.form are safely bound as parameters.

SQL injection via f-string interpolation. User-supplied username and password from request.form are directly embedded into the SQL query string: f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '{username}' AND password = '{password}'". An attacker can bypass authentication or extract data with payloads like ' OR '1'='1' --.

SQL injection via f-string interpolation in transaction search: query = f"SELECT * FROM \"transaction\" WHERE ... AND description LIKE '%{search_term}%'". The search_term from request.args is directly interpolated, allowing UNION-based extraction of data from other tables.

Credit card numbers (CCN) are exposed in the /fetch/customer API response. The customer_dict includes 'cc_num': customer_record.ccn, returning full credit card numbers in plaintext JSON responses without masking or truncation.

Missing negative amount validation in transfer: amount = Decimal(str(data.get('amount', 0))) accepts negative values. A negative transfer amount would reverse the money flow, effectively stealing money from the recipient. No minimum/maximum amount checks exist.

Application runs with debug=True in the Application constructor. Debug mode can expose verbose error messages, stack traces, and internal application state to end users, aiding attackers in reconnaissance.
Hardcoded credentials: admin/123456, john/Password, tim/Vaider2. Weak default passwords for user accounts stored in source code.
User input encoded to bytes and passed to pickle.loads(), which can execute arbitrary code via crafted pickle payloads

Attacker-controlled uploaded file bytes (req._params['upload'].file.read(), line 24) are concatenated into a shell command string (cmd = 'echo ' + str(user_input[:10]), line 28) and passed to os.system(cmd) at line 29 with no sanitization. The /file-upload route (line 82) is reachable and unauthenticated; shell metacharacters (backticks, ;, $()) within the first 10 bytes enable arbitrary OS command execution. GT covers analogous cmdi sinks in apps/fastapi_app.py and apps/flask_app.py but had no entry for apps/falcon_app.py.

X-XSS-Protection header explicitly set to 0 by default, disabling the browser's built-in XSS filter. While this header is deprecated in modern browsers, it actively removes a defense layer in older browsers.
User passwords from USERS_XML are inserted into SQLite database in plaintext without any hashing via cursor.executemany — extractable via SQL injection

The deleteAllPastes GraphQL query deletes every paste in the database (Paste.query.delete()) without any authentication or authorization check. Any unauthenticated user can invoke this query to destroy all application data.

BFLA (Broken Function Level Authorization) on the delete-user API endpoint. The @token_required decorator is commented out (lines 221-222), so DELETE /api/v1/delete-user/<user_id> can be called by anyone without authentication to delete any user from the database.

User-controlled query parameter 'user_input' is read in ThreadView.on_get via req.get_param('user_input') (line 73) on the /thread route (registered line 83) and passed to thread_function via threading.Thread(args=(user_input,)). Inside thread_function it is concatenated into a shell command cmd = 'echo ' + str(user_input) (line 63) and executed with os.system(cmd) (line 64) with no sanitization, enabling arbitrary OS command execution. This is a distinct sink from the apps/fastapi_app.py (vulnpy-077) and trigger-module cmdi entries; apps/falcon_app.py was not previously labeled.
